title: Whatever You Do, Don't Blame the Kids
author: Caracappa, Michele
summary: Responding to a Chalkbeat report on declining book-reading among New York students, the author challenges the assumption that scarce time for whole novels reflects students' motivation or ability rather than systemic choices. Drawing on researcher Cynthia Coburn's work on how a policy problem's framing determines which solutions seem viable, she argues that quoting teachers saying kids 'simply cannot handle' whole texts locates the problem inside students rather than in instructional-time allocation, mandated pacing, and intervention curricula that crowd out full-length books. The piece contends this framing is self-defeating because it removes the incentive to fix curriculum and time allocation in the first place. Rather than relying on individual teachers to make exceptions, the author calls for system-wide policy guaranteeing every student access to curricula built around whole, high-quality texts - as some NYC-Reads-adopted curricula already do and others do not - and argues this should be as non-negotiable a policy priority as the city's recent sweeping rules on AI and devices in classrooms.
points: Reject 'kids can't handle it' framing of declining book-reading; how a problem is framed determines which policy solutions seem viable.
Push for system-wide curriculum policy that guarantees access to high-quality, full-length texts rather than relying on individual teachers to make exceptions.
Audit adopted curricula against a clear bar for whole-book engagement rather than accepting marketing claims of 'high-quality.'
Treat the speed with which districts act on AI/device policy as a template for acting just as quickly on guaranteeing access to whole texts.
Preserve the personal agency individual teachers show (assigning novels despite the odds) while still pursuing structural, system-level fixes.
quotes: Even if she had time to teach a book, the veteran teacher said, her students either have no interest in reading or barely know how.
By framing the problem through the lens of students’ inability, I worry we trap ourselves within a self-defeating cycle.
how a policy problem is framed is important because it assigns responsibility and creates rationales that authorize some policy solutions and not others.
If we never teach them a novel, then shame on us because we’re the ones who are not giving them the opportunity to build those skills.
it’s both unfair and impractical to ask teachers to shift policy and practice one classroom at a time.
This should be a fundamental guarantee regardless of zip code or district boundary.
